units.name: 151 The Invisible Push
units.passage: Human brains are drawn to surprises. Once a situation turns routine and foreseeable, our enthusiasm cools, and our focus drifts toward whatever is fresh. Neuroscientists trace both this restlessness and the burst of pleasure that novelty brings to a mechanism called reward prediction error. Without noticing it, we are always forecasting what will happen next, for instance, roughly what amount should appear on the screen when we look up our bank balance at a cash machine. If the actual figure turns out larger than we guessed, say by a hundred dollars, our forecast has been wrong in a pleasant way, and this welcome mistake prompts the release of dopamine, a neurotransmitter associated with reward and drive. What sets off the chemical is not the additional cash as such but the excitement of good news nobody predicted. Indeed, the bare possibility of such an error can be enough to switch dopamine on. Picture yourself on your usual route to the office when you notice a bakery that has just opened; you feel a spark of delight before sampling a single croissant or even stepping inside. Dopamine is in charge here, producing a sensation separate from physical pleasure, one fueled by expectation and the chance of finding something new and possibly better.

items.q: 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Routine Makes Us Feel Safe and Calm
Never Trust Your Predictions About Money
Surprise and the Brain: How Prediction Errors Release Dopamine
The Hard Work Required to Try Unfamiliar Things
Sensory Pleasure as the Key to Daily Happiness
items.exp: 예측보다 좋은 결과가 생길 때(보상 예측 오류) 도파민이 분비되어 새로움에 끌린다는 내용이에요.

items.q: 글의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?
choices: 도파민은 늘어난 돈의 액수 자체에 반응하여 분비된다.
상황이 예측 가능해지면 흥미가 줄어든다.
우리는 다음에 일어날 일을 끊임없이 예측한다.
도파민은 보상 및 동기와 관련된 신경 전달 물질이다.
예측 오류의 가능성만으로도 도파민이 작동할 수 있다.
items.exp: 도파민을 촉발하는 것은 추가된 돈 자체가 아니라(not the additional cash as such) 예상치 못한 좋은 소식의 흥분이라고 했어요.

items.q: 새로 문을 연 빵집의 예가 보여 주는 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 빵의 맛이 좋을수록 도파민이 더 많이 나온다.
익숙한 길을 걸을 때 뇌는 가장 큰 즐거움을 느낀다.
출근길에는 새로운 것에 주의를 기울이기 어렵다.
감각적 즐거움이 있어야만 기대감이 생긴다.
직접 맛보기 전에도 새로움의 가능성만으로 기대감이 생긴다.
items.exp: 빵을 맛보거나 안에 들어가기 전에도 기쁨을 느끼며, 이는 감각적 즐거움과 다른 기대감에서 나온다고 했어요.

items.q: 지문의 the [bare] possibility에서 bare의 문맥상 의미로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: uncovered
mere
scarcely visible
honest
complete
items.exp: '그런 오류의 가능성만으로도' 도파민이 작동한다는 뜻이므로 bare는 mere(단지 ~만의)의 의미예요.

items.q: 지문의 문장 '[What] sets off the chemical is not the additional cash as such but the excitement of good news nobody predicted.'의 What과 쓰임이 같은 것은?
choices: What time does the store close?
What a surprising result it was!
What do you think about the idea?
What she told me turned out to be true.
What if the plan fails?
items.exp: 지문의 What은 '~하는 것'이라는 뜻의 관계대명사로, 명사절을 이끌어 주어 역할을 해요. 같은 쓰임은 What she told me예요.

items.q: 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: how the brain's prediction errors turn novelty into pleasure
the role of dopamine in producing physical pleasure
why people should avoid routine in daily life
the dangers of overestimating one's bank balance
how expectation reduces the brain's need for reward
items.exp: 예측이 좋은 쪽으로 틀릴 때(reward prediction error) 도파민이 분비되어 새로움이 즐거움으로 이어진다는 글이에요. 도파민은 physical pleasure와 separate한 감각을 만든다고 했으니 ②는 아니에요.

items.q: Which of the following is true according to the passage?
choices: Our focus naturally stays on familiar things rather than fresh ones.
Dopamine is released only after a reward has actually been received.
Neuroscientists believe restlessness and the pleasure of novelty have unrelated causes.
Dopamine produces a feeling that is distinct from physical pleasure.
The pleasure of a surprise depends on the size of the unexpected gain.
items.exp: 마지막 문장에서 도파민이 producing a sensation separate from physical pleasure라고 했어요. 두 현상은 같은 기제(reward prediction error)로 설명되고, 가능성만으로도(the bare possibility) 도파민이 켜진다고 했어요.

items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Because the brain constantly (A) ___ what comes next, an outcome better than anticipated releases dopamine, so the mere (B) ___ of something new can produce delight before any reward is received.
choices: (A) ignores — (B) memory
(A) predicts — (B) prospect
(A) predicts — (B) cost
(A) remembers — (B) prospect
(A) controls — (B) absence
items.exp: we are always forecasting what will happen next이므로 (A)는 predicts, 빵집에 들어가기도 전에 the chance of finding something new로 기쁨을 느끼므로 (B)는 prospect(가능성)예요.

items.q: 밑줄 친 [this welcome mistake]가 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은? (If the actual figure turns out larger than we guessed, say by a hundred dollars, our forecast has been wrong in a pleasant way, and [this welcome mistake] prompts the release of dopamine, a neurotransmitter associated with reward and drive.)
choices: an error made by the bank in our favor
a prediction that turned out to be too optimistic
a forecast that fell short of a pleasant reality
the habit of spending more than we planned
a failure to check our balance regularly
items.exp: our forecast has been wrong in a pleasant way, 즉 실제 액수가 예측보다 커서 예측이 '기분 좋게 틀린' 것을 가리켜요. 은행의 실수가 아니라 우리의 예측 오류예요.

items.q: 다음 중 글의 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: our enthusiasm [cools], and our focus drifts
the burst of pleasure that novelty [brings]
our forecast has been wrong in a [pleasant] way
producing a sensation [separate] from physical pleasure
one fueled by [indifference] and the chance of finding something new
items.exp: 도파민이 만드는 감각은 기대와 새로움의 가능성으로 채워지는 것이므로 indifference(무관심)가 아니라 expectation이어야 해요.

units.name: 152 The Leap of Sapiens
units.passage: What makes human language truly special is not that it carries information. Its distinctive power lies instead in conveying information about things that are entirely absent from the world. So far as researchers can tell, Sapiens alone can discuss beings they have never seen, heard, or touched. Legends, myths, deities, and religions first emerged during a cognitive leap that took place roughly 70,000 years ago, and this capacity to talk about fictions became the hallmark of Sapiens speech. Fiction, of course, carries real dangers, since it can mislead and distract. Someone who heads into the woods in search of fairies and unicorns is less likely to survive than someone hunting for mushrooms and deer. Despite such risks, fiction has allowed us not only to imagine but to imagine together. Communities across the globe spin comparable myths, including the creation account of the Bible, the Dreamtime stories of Aboriginal Australians, and even the modern myths that shape our everyday routines. Such shared stories grant Sapiens an unprecedented capacity: the power to cooperate flexibly with vast numbers of strangers who believe in the same things.

items.q: 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Language: Simply a Tool for Passing On Facts
Why Myths Differ So Much Across Cultures
The Dangers of Myths to Human Survival
Fairies and Unicorns: Ancient Beliefs of Sapiens
Shared Fictions: The Root of Large-Scale Human Cooperation
items.exp: 허구를 말하는 능력이 사피엔스 언어의 특징이며, 공유된 신화가 수많은 낯선 사람과의 협력을 가능하게 했다는 내용이에요.

items.q: 글의 내용과 일치하는 것은?
choices: 언어의 고유한 특징은 정보를 전달하는 능력 그 자체이다.
전설, 신화, 종교는 약 7만 년 전 인지 도약 시기에 처음 나타났다.
허구는 인간의 생존에 아무런 위험도 주지 않는다.
신화는 일부 지역 사회에서만 만들어졌다.
현대 사회에는 더 이상 신화가 존재하지 않는다.
items.exp: Legends, myths, deities, and religions first emerged during a cognitive leap ... roughly 70,000 years ago라고 했어요.

items.q: 숲에서 요정과 유니콘을 찾는 사람의 예가 보여 주는 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 상상력이 풍부할수록 생존에 유리하다는 점
버섯과 사슴이 초기 인류의 주식이었다는 점
신화가 사람들을 하나로 묶는다는 점
허구가 사람을 잘못 이끌어 생존에 불리할 수 있다는 점
사피엔스만이 숲에서 사냥할 수 있었다는 점
items.exp: 허구는 사람을 오도하고 주의를 흐트러뜨릴 수 있다는 위험의 예로, 요정을 찾는 사람이 살아남을 가능성이 더 낮다고 했어요.

items.q: 지문의 the [hallmark] of Sapiens speech에서 hallmark의 문맥상 의미로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: a distinguishing feature
an official stamp on gold
a sudden turning point
a written historical record
a serious weakness
items.exp: 허구에 대해 말하는 능력이 사피엔스 언어를 '규정하는 특징'이 되었다는 뜻이에요.

items.q: 지문의 문장 'Despite such risks, fiction has allowed us not only to imagine but to imagine together.'에 대한 설명으로 옳은 것은?
choices: Despite는 접속사이므로 뒤에 절이 와야 한다.
allowed us to imagine은 allowed us imagining으로 바꿔도 어법상 맞다.
not only A but B 구문으로, A보다 B에 초점을 둔다.
has allowed는 현재완료이므로 yesterday와 함께 쓸 수 있다.
together는 형용사로 앞의 명사를 수식한다.
items.exp: not only A but (also) B는 'A뿐만 아니라 B도'의 뜻으로 B(함께 상상하기)를 강조해요. Despite는 전치사이고, allow는 목적격보어로 to부정사를 써요.

items.q: 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: how language evolved to transmit factual information
the dangers of believing in fairies and unicorns
the differences among the world's creation myths
the survival skills of early human hunters
the unique ability of Sapiens to share fictions and cooperate
items.exp: 사피엔스만이 존재하지 않는 것에 대해 말할 수 있고, 공유된 허구가 the power to cooperate flexibly with vast numbers of strangers를 준다는 내용이에요. 위험(②)은 일부 소재일 뿐이에요.

items.q: Which of the following is true according to the passage?
choices: Animals other than Sapiens can also discuss things they have never perceived.
The author regards fiction as having no downside at all.
The Bible's creation account and Aboriginal Dreamtime stories are cited as comparable myths.
Fiction has mainly enabled individuals to imagine alone.
Cooperation among Sapiens is limited to small groups of acquaintances.
items.exp: Communities across the globe spin comparable myths, including the creation account of the Bible, the Dreamtime stories of Aboriginal Australians라고 했어요. 허구는 real dangers가 있고, 함께 상상하게 하며, 수많은 낯선 이와의 협력을 가능하게 해요.

items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

What distinguishes human language is its capacity to describe the (A) ___, and although such fictions can mislead, believing in them collectively enables (B) ___ among huge numbers of unrelated people.
choices: (A) nonexistent — (B) cooperation
(A) visible — (B) competition
(A) nonexistent — (B) conflict
(A) factual — (B) cooperation
(A) dangerous — (B) isolation
items.exp: conveying information about things that are entirely absent from the world이므로 (A)는 nonexistent, 같은 것을 믿는 낯선 이들과 cooperate flexibly하게 해 준다고 했으니 (B)는 cooperation이에요.

items.q: 다음 문장의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은? (Such shared stories grant Sapiens an unprecedented capacity: the power to cooperate flexibly with vast numbers of strangers ___.)
choices: who share the same bloodline
who believe in the same things
who have never heard of fiction
who hunt in the same forests
who speak different languages
items.exp: 앞에서 shared stories, 즉 함께 믿는 신화가 협력을 가능하게 한다고 했으므로 '같은 것을 믿는' 낯선 사람들(strangers who believe in the same things)이 자연스러워요.

items.q: 다음 중 글의 문장을 옮긴 것으로 어법상 틀린 것은?
choices: [conveying] information about things that are entirely absent
Sapiens alone can discuss beings they [have] never seen
a cognitive leap that [took] place roughly 70,000 years ago
Communities across the globe [spins] comparable myths
is less likely to survive than someone [hunting] for mushrooms
items.exp: 주어가 복수 명사 Communities이므로 동사는 spin이어야 해요(across the globe는 수식어). 나머지는 전치사 뒤 동명사, 현재완료, 과거시제, 명사를 수식하는 현재분사로 모두 맞아요.

units.name: 153 Capital
units.passage: Money may or may not be part of the picture, but every economy must solve the same basic problems: connecting those who give with those who receive, acknowledging and rewarding what people contribute, and organizing those contributions over distance and time so that they produce value no single person could create alone. These tasks match the three classic roles of money, namely serving as a medium of exchange, a unit of account, and a store of value. Increasingly, however, communities are finding quasi-monetary or entirely non-monetary means of accomplishing the same ends. Consider open-source software. There, P2P (peer-to-peer) tools let a network of programmers imagine new projects, pool their skills, and credit each member's input, and none of this requires cash. In a sense, the respect a programmer earns from colleagues, built on how good and how plentiful his or her past contributions have been, works as a kind of currency: it gives experienced contributors a stronger and more durable voice in collective decisions than newcomers enjoy. Yet this esteem is never measured in numbers, nor could it be without losing what makes it valuable. Turning it into figures would be like transferring an analog recording into digital form, a process in which the warmth and human feel of the original slip away.

items.q: 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 화폐를 쓰지 않고도 경제의 핵심 기능이 실현될 수 있다.
기여의 양보다 질이 집단 내 영향력을 결정한다.
비화폐적 대안이 기존 화폐를 곧 대체할 것이다.
P2P 환경에서도 기여는 금전으로 보상해야 효율적이다.
동료의 존경은 수치화하여 경제적 자산으로 활용할 수 있다.
items.exp: 경제의 기본 과제가 화폐의 세 기능과 같으며, 오픈소스 공동체처럼 돈 없이도 이를 달성하는 방식이 늘고 있다는 내용이에요.

items.q: 글의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?
choices: 경제의 기본 과제는 주는 사람과 받는 사람을 연결하는 것을 포함한다.
화폐의 세 가지 기능은 교환의 매개, 계산 단위, 가치 저장이다.
오픈소스 프로그래머들은 돈 없이도 협업하고 기여를 인정한다.
동료들의 존경은 수치로 정확히 측정되어 기록된다.
경험 많은 기여자는 집단 결정에 더 큰 영향력을 가진다.
items.exp: 이 존경은 숫자로 측정되지 않으며(never measured in numbers), 수치화하면 그 가치를 잃는다고 했어요.

items.q: 오픈소스 공동체에서 화폐의 역할을 대신하는 것으로 글에 제시된 것은?
choices: 프로그램 판매 수익
프로젝트 참여 기간
동료들로부터 얻는 존경
공동체 운영자의 승인
디지털 녹음 기술
items.exp: 동료들에게서 얻는 존경(the respect a programmer earns from colleagues)이 일종의 화폐로 작용한다고 했어요.

items.q: 지문의 a stronger and more [durable] voice에서 durable의 문맥상 의미로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: fragile
temporary
physical
official
lasting
items.exp: 경험 많은 기여자가 집단 결정에 더 강하고 '오래 지속되는' 영향력을 가진다는 뜻이므로 lasting이에요.

items.q: 지문의 문장 'Yet this esteem is never measured in numbers, [nor could it be] without losing what makes it valuable.'의 밑줄 친 부분과 같은 어순 원리가 적용된 것은?
choices: She has never been abroad, and I haven't either.
He didn't attend the meeting, and neither did his boss.
Not knowing the answer, I kept silent.
I don't know where he lives.
If it rains, we will stay home.
items.exp: nor/neither가 앞에 오면 <(조)동사 + 주어> 어순으로 도치돼요. neither did his boss가 같은 원리예요.

items.q: 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Money's Three Roles and Why They Never Change
Open-Source Software: A Threat to Traditional Banking
Why Digital Recordings Sound Worse Than Analog
Reputation as Currency: Non-Monetary Economies in Action
How Programmers Can Earn More Cash Online
items.exp: 오픈소스 공동체에서 동료의 존경이 works as a kind of currency하며, 돈 없이 경제의 기본 과제를 해결하는 예라는 글이에요. 아날로그·디지털 비유(③)는 보조 설명일 뿐이에요.

items.q: According to the passage, what determines the respect a programmer earns from colleagues?
choices: the number of years spent in formal education
the quality and quantity of his or her past contributions
the amount of money invested in the project
votes cast by newcomers to the network
the official rank assigned by project leaders
items.exp: 존경은 built on how good and how plentiful his or her past contributions have been, 즉 과거 기여의 질과 양에 바탕을 둔다고 했어요.

items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

The fundamental tasks of any economy, which correspond to the classic functions of money, can be met through (A) ___ means such as peer respect, whose value would be lost if it were (B) ___.
choices: (A) non-monetary — (B) quantified
(A) financial — (B) shared
(A) non-monetary — (B) earned
(A) governmental — (B) quantified
(A) digital — (B) recorded
items.exp: quasi-monetary or entirely non-monetary means로 같은 목적을 이루며, 존경은 never measured in numbers, nor could it be without losing what makes it valuable이므로 수치화(quantified)되면 가치를 잃어요.

items.q: 밑줄 친 [the warmth and human feel of the original slip away]가 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은? (Turning it into figures would be like transferring an analog recording into digital form, a process in which [the warmth and human feel of the original slip away].)
choices: Digital tools make collaboration less efficient.
Experienced contributors gradually lose their influence.
Old recordings are more valuable than new software.
Programmers prefer cash rewards to recognition.
Reducing esteem to numbers would strip it of what makes it meaningful.
items.exp: Turning it into figures, 즉 존경을 숫자로 바꾸는 일을 아날로그 녹음의 디지털 변환에 비유해, 그 과정에서 본래의 가치(what makes it valuable)가 사라진다는 뜻이에요.

items.q: 다음 중 글의 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: connecting those who give with those who [receive]
[acknowledging] and rewarding what people contribute
and [all] of this requires cash

units.name: 154 Traces of the Past
units.passage: Until about 2000, museums commonly put on display objects whose provenance was uncertain, and in doing so they lent a kind of respectability to antiquities that might otherwise have been regarded as illegally acquired. Such pieces typically had no documentation, had surfaced on the market only recently, and came with circumstances that pointed to looting. Critics labeled this practice antiquities laundering. The term did not mean that public display changed who legally owned the objects; rather, it meant that exhibition and scholarly publication bestowed a somewhat deceptive legitimacy on items that might well have been stolen. Through such activities, museums were indirectly feeding a cycle of destruction at archaeological sites. A well-known illustration is the Euphronios Krater, a prized Greek vase dating from the 6th century BC, which the Metropolitan Museum of Art purchased in 1972. The vessel had no reliable record of its origin, and investigators later discovered that it had been dug up illegally in Italy, a finding that provoked broad international alarm. After years of dispute, the museum finally sent the krater back to Italy in 2008. The episode revealed how prestigious institutions, simply by displaying objects of unknown origin, could give looted artifacts an air of legitimacy and endanger cultural heritage.

units.name: 155 Tourism Today
units.passage: Traditional religious institutions, which once offered moral space, both in the mind and as physical places where people could reflect and seek moral guidance, have lost much of their influence. In their place, a post-conventional society has developed sites that encourage open dialogue among people holding different perspectives, and these new spaces are seen as playing a key role in forming contemporary ideas of morality. Amid this shift, dark tourism, which involves traveling to places of historical tragedy such as the Killing Fields or Auschwitz, has drawn interest as a setting in which visitors confront painful pasts and come to view morality from many angles. People go to these locations to learn about history, to reflect morally, and to honor the victims, which suggests that such sites could serve as arenas for moral contemplation, carried out through reflection and conversation, instead of traditional institutions. Dark tourism, however, is not free from ethical problems, particularly when a site is turned into a business, presents history inaccurately, or is treated without respect. Wrestling with these dilemmas pushes individuals to think critically about values such as empathy, responsibility, and justice. In this way, dark tourism can act as a moral forum for today's society, a place where people remember what happened and explore moral understanding in present-day contexts.

units.name: 156 Language’s Many Faces
units.passage: According to the French philosopher Merleau-Ponty, language does not spring solely from the human body; it arises from the whole sensory world we inhabit. And since we participate in language as members of this shared world, so do animals and all other creatures. For him, language is a form of life, belonging not just to us but to everything around us. On this view, the intricacy of human speech reflects the intricacy of the Earth's ecosystems rather than that of our own species, since language is, in essence, the voice of trees, waves, and forests. It follows that as technological civilization reduces the variety of life on the planet, language itself grows poorer. Songbirds, for instance, are vanishing from the skies as their habitats are destroyed, so our speech can no longer draw nourishment from the rhythms of their songs. Likewise, as one river after another is blocked by dams and its splashing voice falls silent, our languages become steadily thinner and lighter, gradually drained of the resonance they once drew from the earth.

units.name: 157 Reasoning Errors
units.passage: Preset options exert a quiet pull on us. Like a cushion we sink into without thinking, a default spares us mental effort and reduces the strain of deciding, which is why people who struggle to make up their minds find it especially welcome. Designers of policies and products can therefore steer behavior simply by building a default into a choice, while still leaving people free to pick something else. Part of the reason this works is that, when faced with a choice between an unfamiliar option and a familiar one, humans lean strongly toward caution, even when switching would clearly pay off. Consider how many computer owners keep using whatever browser came installed on their machines, for example Edge on a Windows PC, although rivals like Chrome or Firefox might be faster, safer, or richer in features. Remarkably, this pull operates even when nobody has explicitly set a standard option for us. In those situations, our own previous behavior becomes the default, thereby extending the current state of affairs indefinitely. To take a personal case, my bank bills me every year for sending paper statements, a fee I could avoid at once by choosing digital ones. Yet although the charge has irritated me for years, I have never gotten around to canceling it.

units.name: 158 The Power of Evaluation
units.passage: As companies grow used to working in teams that pursue constant improvement and track measurable results, conventional ways of appraising staff, such as the yearly review of each individual, are being reconsidered, and some firms are abandoning them altogether. One reason for this shift is the worry that judging workers one by one weakened cooperation, since it rewarded personal achievement at the expense of the group. In response, many organizations have adopted gainsharing and other schemes that link pay to team results; under such plans, members divide among themselves the money saved through greater output or through cutting mistakes and waste. Still, moving to a team-based model hardly makes individual accountability disappear. Workers frequently carry out tasks on their own even as they cooperate toward common aims. Typically, each person holds a clearly defined role, performed alone yet feeding into what the team is trying to accomplish. For this reason, team members need to understand exactly what they are responsible for and to find their tasks demanding. They also help decide which measures will serve as the benchmarks of good performance, and cooperation tends to improve when each member is asked to evaluate how well his or her own work fits the team's goals.

units.name: 159 Beyond the Utilitarian
units.passage: We usually narrate the past as a long struggle over essentials rather than indulgences: the struggle for liberty, for equal rights, for security, for the power to rule ourselves. Yet the story of pleasure deserves attention as well, because many discoveries that looked frivolous at first went on to reshape history. Coffee offers a vivid case. Thanks to its energizing effect and attractive flavor, Europeans drank more and more of it during the 1600s, and this surge gave birth to the coffeehouse. In London across the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, such places, St. James's Coffee House among them, functioned in practice as newsrooms, where political news spread from table to table and public debate took form. Early magazines such as The Tatler went so far as to name specific coffeehouses as the origin of their stories. In this way, these gathering spots built the institutional groundwork on which modern journalism would rest. The lesson is broader than coffee: when people invent and share experiences meant to give pleasure or wonder, they frequently end up changing society more profoundly than those who concern themselves only with practical needs.

units.name: 160 Storytelling Through Different Eyes
units.passage: Literature's early experiments with child narrators deserve a close look, partly because of their artistic quality and lasting impact, but also because critics have aimed harsh accusations at the device. Penny Brown, an expert on nineteenth-century English fiction, argues that Victorian writers who tried to adopt a child's point of view seldom succeeded, since their work tends to reflect the writer's own peculiar, personal image of childhood and can seem simply sweet or awkward. Yet this complaint about excessive sentimentality is gentle next to the charges brought by critics who regard children's literature as a kind of colonization. Among all the methods adults use to shape and control young readers, these critics claim, a child narrator works most quietly yet persuasively, because it lets the author hide his or her presence and intentions while speaking to the child, which makes it far easier for readers to identify with the voice on the page. Put differently, authors place a child in the storyteller's seat as a stand-in so that young readers are led, without realizing it, to accept an adult-made image of how children ought to be.

units.name: 161 Buried Stories
units.passage: The layers that make up the Earth are limited; every one of them starts, continues, and finishes. As wind and rain, slow wearing away, and human activity strip the planet one layer at a time, fossils come to light, showing how life on Earth developed. But who finds these remains, and why, raises an entirely different debate. Those who search for fossils divide into two camps: paleontologists and commercial collectors. Paleontologists, who go through years of demanding academic training, insist that fossils must be kept out of the marketplace. Commercial dealers, by contrast, claim they are rescuing specimens that erosion would otherwise destroy, and that their work supports teaching, scientific study, and public curiosity. Even so, however much field experience they have gained on their own, the self-described 'commercial paleontologists' are not genuine paleontologists. The irony is that the science itself was founded by amateur lovers of natural history, well before the term paleontology had even been coined. It then grew into one of the most visible fields with a commercial side, a side that angers scientists while also earning a rightful place among the great achievements of discovery.

units.name: 162 How Marketing Shapes Us
units.passage: Marketing images of charming wild animals rely on the creatures' attractive features to stir particular feelings in viewers, with the goal of prompting donations to conservation groups or boosting bookings for safari trips. Such pictures, however, do little to make us think critically about the unequal power, the exclusions, and the injustices that structure relations between people and animals. In addition, commercial digital environments in which humans and animals meet lead us to ignore the ties and common ecosystems linking every living thing. Because this habit of not seeing has been learned and limits how we imagine ecological and political life, some people have started asking how visual depictions determine what catches our eye and what escapes it. This approach seeks to bring the ordinary encounters between species into view and to rouse us from our profound unawareness. Consider a documentary that shows rescued wild animals as touching stories while also exploring the ecological and political background behind them, for example the destruction of habitats or the illegal wildlife trade. Such a film demonstrates what a fuller perspective looks like. By connecting emotional appeal to these wider problems, it encourages audiences to reflect on the deeper causes of environmental damage instead of dwelling only on comforting rescue tales.

units.name: 163 Statistical Data
units.passage: Hedonic scores have become a fixture of the food industry because they are easy to collect, reasonably precise, and widely accepted, yet this convenience has drawn attention away from how awkward it really is to turn liking into a number. Two kinds of problems persist. One is semantic: a label such as "like slightly" does not mean the same thing to every taster. The other is mathematical: a rating of eight does not represent double the pleasure of a rating of four, since the scale is not built on equal units of enjoyment. Worse, even the seemingly straightforward act of asking people about their preferences turns out to be tricky. Take the popular "just about right" (JAR) scale, which tries to pin down the ideal strength of a single feature of a product. Participants taste a series of samples that differ in only one respect—say, the amount of sugar added, which serves as the independent variable—and point to the one that strikes them as neither excessive nor insufficient. The catch is subtle but stubborn: the sweetness level people label as ideal often fails to match the sweetness level they say they enjoy most. Spend enough time studying how preference is measured, and a near-universal rule starts to emerge: things are seldom quite as good, or as bad, as they first appear.

units.name: 164 What Is Niche?
units.passage: For a long time, scientists assumed that regions rich in biodiversity were breeding grounds for new zoonotic pathogens and therefore posed a particular danger to people. More recent work, however, shows that in certain circumstances a wealth of species can actually reduce the spread of diseases that pass from animals to humans. This may sound contradictory, yet a few principles stand out. Intact ecosystems function as promoters of health, keeping pathogens confined within their natural settings. The reason is that predators and rival species hold disease-carrying populations in check, which makes it less likely that a pathogen will spill over into human communities. When biodiversity declines, on the other hand, fresh ecological niches open up, and these vacancies can be filled by pathogens, hosts, vectors, and substitute reservoir species. As certain species disappear, the survivors that flourish—rats and bats are typical cases—tend to be the very animals most likely to carry dangerous microbes capable of jumping to humans. The growing incidence of Lyme disease in the United States illustrates this pattern well. There, broken food chains led to fewer predators such as foxes and owls, so white-footed mice, the main hosts of the Lyme bacterium, multiplied rapidly. More mice meant more infected ticks, and more infected ticks meant a higher chance that people would catch the disease.

units.name: 165 The Hidden Guide to the Mind
units.passage: Because I study procrastination for a living, reporters and bloggers frequently contact me hoping to figure out why people put things off. Most of them approach the topic as a question of managing time or summoning willpower, and I use these conversations as a chance to correct such widespread myths. Despite what many assume, putting tasks off does not stem from laziness, an inability to concentrate, or weak self-control. Rather, it comes down to handling our moods poorly. Fundamentally, procrastination is a way of escaping—not from the work itself, but from the feelings tied to it. When we expect a job to bring unease, worry, or doubts about our own competence, those expected feelings can become so intense that steering clear of the task feels like the most urgent goal, even though doing so will cost us later. Since emotions frequently defy logic, such a response is entirely understandable. Procrastination, in other words, is less a breakdown of self-discipline than a profound emotional reaction to work we find upsetting. Recognizing this is essential if we want to tackle the habit at its source rather than merely treating its symptoms.

units.name: 166 The Quality of What We Do
units.passage: After I had tuned my motorcycle countless times, the job has turned into a kind of ritual, so I no longer have to stop and think about each step. Zen Buddhists speak of "just sitting," a practice in which the boundary between the self and its object dissolves. In much the same spirit, I can regard working on my motorcycle as "just fixing," an activity in which the machine and I become one. When I am no longer ruled by a sense of being apart from the thing in front of me, it is fair to say that I care about it. Caring, in this sense, means identifying with the work itself, and once I reach that state, caring reveals another face: quality. Quality, then, is not something added to a task from the outside; it grows out of this sense of unity. The lesson applies to every kind of work, not just repairs. What matters most is to nurture a calm state of mind that removes the line separating me from everything around me. Out of that calm, values emerge without force. They, in turn, lead me to reason clearly and to behave well, and whatever I make or do in that condition is more than a mere outcome—it is a visible sign of harmony within.

units.name: 167 Mobility
units.passage: In road traffic, active errors are the slips people make on the spot—driving too fast, stepping on the wrong pedal, or heading the wrong way down a one-way road. Latent errors, by contrast, are flaws buried in the system itself, such as long straight roads and generous lanes that tempt drivers to go faster. According to one journalist, these hidden flaws are the biggest danger to the safety of any complex system, yet they are notoriously hard to measure. The Swiss cheese model shows why. Picture latent errors as the holes in a pile of cheese slices. An accident happens only when the holes happen to line up, letting an active error slip all the way through. Think about a driver turning right at a crossroads. Usually the holes fail to match up: no one may be crossing, or the driver may have enough time to look around. When the design flaws do line up perfectly, though, a driver can "accidentally" bring about a disaster. Because latent errors are by nature difficult to notice, it is the active error that stands out; it is what investigators document and study. Overlooking the hidden flaws leaves us spinning our wheels, never achieving genuine gains in road safety.

units.name: 168 Nature’s Smart Moves
units.passage: Deception is far older than humanity. Animals regularly trick one another by playing on each other's senses and perceptions. Consider two male deer competing for a mate or a patch of territory. Neither stag gains from letting the dispute turn into an all-out fight, so their contest unfolds through a series of ritual displays in which each tries to convince the other that it would come out on top in a real battle. Judging a rival's actual strength correctly matters, but each animal also profits if it can fool the other into overestimating its power. Suppose two deer are roughly matched in strength. If one is misled into believing its rival is mightier and retreats, the rival claims victory without paying the price of a dangerous fight. As a result, natural selection favors tactics that plant false impressions in the minds of competitors. This pressure, however, cuts both ways: an animal benefits from deceiving others, but it benefits just as much from not being fooled itself. Animals therefore evolve ways to test whether a rival's signals are honest, setting off a coevolutionary arms race, with the skill of misleading and the skill of seeing through deception evolving side by side.

units.name: 169 Law of Wealth
units.passage: The French economist Thomas Piketty summarizes a basic tendency of capitalism with the formula r > g, in which r stands for the return earned on capital and g for the growth of the whole economy. Whenever r stays above g for a long stretch, the fortunes of those who already own assets swell more quickly than national output, so the distance between rich and poor keeps widening. This mechanism, Piketty argues, accounts for the extreme concentration of wealth in the nineteenth century and helps explain why the French Revolution only partly succeeded. The revolutionary assemblies did introduce a tax that every citizen had to pay, whatever his rank, but it was set at a trivial level—only one or two percent on inherited property—and thus did almost nothing to slow the growth of private fortunes relative to the economy. With capital yielding roughly five percent a year while output rose by barely one percent, it is hardly surprising that France, even in the prosperous Belle Époque under a republic, remained as unequal as Britain, which was still ruled by a monarch. What kept the gap alive, then, was not whether the state called itself a republic or a kingdom but its failure to build a tax system capable of offsetting r > g.

items.exp: 'a tax that every citizen had to pay, whatever his rank'에서 신분과 관계없는 세금을 도입했음을 알 수 있어요. 세율은 1~2퍼센트였고, 프랑스는 영국만큼 불평등했어요.

items.q: 글에 따르면 19세기 프랑스의 자본 수익률과 경제 성장률이 바르게 짝지어진 것은? (자본 수익률 – 경제 성장률)

items.q: 글에 쓰인 trivial의 문맥상 의미로 가장 알맞은 것은?
choices: fair and reasonable
very small and unimportant
suddenly increased
hard to calculate
widely accepted
items.exp: 세율이 1~2퍼센트에 불과해 격차를 거의 늦추지 못했다고 했으니 trivial은 '아주 작고 하찮은'이라는 뜻이에요.

items.q: 다음 문장의 [밑줄 친 부분]에 대한 설명으로 알맞은 것은? "With capital [yielding] roughly five percent a year while output rose by barely one percent, it is hardly surprising that France ... remained as unequal as Britain."
choices: 앞의 명사 capital을 수식하는 과거분사이다.
동명사로 문장 전체의 주어 역할을 한다.
to yield로 고쳐야 어법상 옳다.

yielded로 고쳐야 어법상 옳다.

items.q: 글의 주제로 가장 알맞은 것은?
choices: the economic advantages of monarchy over republic
how Piketty calculated nineteenth-century growth rates
the role of inheritance in French family life
how a weak tax system, rather than the form of government, kept inequality alive in France
the cultural achievements of the Belle Époque
items.exp: r > g 상황에서 혁명의 세금이 너무 낮아 격차를 줄이지 못했고, 핵심은 'failure to build a tax system'이라는 내용이에요.

items.q: According to the passage, what does r stand for in Piketty's formula?
choices: the return earned on capital
the growth of the whole economy
the rate of tax on inherited property
the share of the population owning assets
the revenue collected by the state

items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Piketty's formula r > g shows that when returns on (A) ___ exceed economic growth, inequality widens, which is why the Revolution's tiny tax did little to stop private fortunes from growing faster than the (B) ___.

(A) capital — (B) economy
(A) capital — (B) monarchy
(A) taxes — (B) revolution
(A) land — (B) population

choices: It introduced a tax that most citizens refused to pay.
It made France far more unequal than Britain.
It ended private ownership of inherited property.
It brought prosperity only to the monarchy.
It changed the form of government but did not stop wealth from concentrating.

items.q: 다음 중 글의 문장을 옮긴 것으로 어법상 틀린 것은?
choices: in which r [stands] for the return earned on capital
the fortunes of those who already own assets [swell] more quickly
Britain, [that] was still ruled by a monarch
a tax that every citizen [had to pay], whatever his rank

units.name: 170 The Beauty of Music
units.passage: Music and ethics are linked chiefly through music's expressive force. That force involves more than conveying feelings; it also lets a listener glimpse what other people are feeling. Grasping, through empathy, how wide and deep the emotions of others—or even our own—can be is central to moral education, because no one can become a better person without growing in this kind of emotional understanding. Yet music may serve morality in a second way as well: by adding to the joy that motivates us to carry out our obligations. Here we can borrow an idea in the spirit of Kant, namely that a cheerful person is more inclined to fulfill a duty than someone who is sad or discouraged. Happiness is neither the aim of moral life nor a condition one must meet before acting rightly; rather, it is a useful tool that strengthens the will to act. Therefore, if listening to music makes people happier, it may quietly reinforce their moral resolve. Seen this way, music does two things at once: it widens our empathetic grasp of others, and it creates a state of mind in which living a good and ethical life becomes less of a struggle.

items.q: 글의 주제로 가장 알맞은 것은?
choices: the history of music in moral philosophy
why happiness is the final goal of ethics
how Kant criticized emotional music
the difficulty of measuring emotions in music
two ways in which music can support moral life
items.exp: 음악은 공감적 이해를 넓히고, 기쁨을 더해 도덕적 의지를 강화한다는 두 가지 방식을 설명해요. 마지막 문장 'music does two things at once'가 이를 정리해요.

items.q: 글의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?
choices: 음악은 감정 표현뿐 아니라 타인의 감정을 엿보게 해 준다.
공감을 통한 감정 이해는 도덕 교육의 핵심이다.
행복은 도덕적 행동을 하기 위한 필수 전제 조건이다.
칸트적 관점에서 기쁜 사람은 의무를 더 잘 이행하는 경향이 있다.
음악은 윤리적으로 살기 덜 힘든 마음 상태를 만들 수 있다.
items.exp: 'Happiness is neither the aim of moral life nor a condition one must meet before acting rightly'라고 했으므로 행복은 필수 전제 조건이 아니에요.

items.q: 글에서 행복의 역할로 설명된 것은?
choices: 도덕적 의지를 강화하는 유용한 도구
도덕적 삶이 추구해야 할 최종 목표
타인의 감정을 판단하는 기준
음악을 감상하기 위한 필수 조건
도덕 교육을 대신하는 수단
items.exp: 'it is a useful tool that strengthens the will to act'에서 행복은 행동하려는 의지를 강화하는 유용한 도구라고 했어요.

items.q: 글에 쓰인 resolve의 문맥상 의미로 가장 알맞은 것은?
choices: a solution to a problem
a formal decision of a group
the act of breaking into parts
firm determination to do something
the final part of a piece of music
items.exp: 음악이 행복을 높여 도덕적 'resolve'를 강화한다는 맥락이므로, 무언가를 하려는 굳은 결심이라는 뜻이에요.

items.q: 다음 문장의 [밑줄 친 부분]에 대한 설명으로 알맞은 것은? "Grasping, through empathy, how wide and deep the emotions of others—or even our own—can be [is] central to moral education."

동명사구 주어(Grasping ~)는 단수 취급하므로 is가 쓰였다.
others가 주어이므로 are로 고쳐야 한다.
being으로 고쳐야 어법상 옳다.
가정법이므로 were로 고쳐야 한다.
items.exp: 문장의 주어는 동명사구 'Grasping ~ can be'이고 동명사구 주어는 단수 취급하므로 is가 맞아요.

items.q: 글의 제목으로 가장 알맞은 것은?
choices: Why Sad Music Makes Us Better People
Music's Two Gifts to Moral Life: Empathy and Joy
Kant's Theory of Musical Beauty
Happiness: The Ultimate Goal of Ethics
How Music Education Replaces Moral Teaching
items.exp: 음악은 'empathetic grasp of others'를 넓히고 기쁨으로 도덕적 의지를 강화한다는 두 역할을 말하므로 공감과 기쁨을 담은 제목이 알맞아요.

items.q: According to the passage, under what condition may music reinforce people's moral resolve?
choices: if it is composed according to Kant's rules
if listening to it makes people happier
if listeners already meet the condition of happiness
if it expresses sadness and discouragement
if it is studied as part of a formal moral education
items.exp: 'if listening to music makes people happier, it may quietly reinforce their moral resolve'라고 했어요.

items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Music supports morality in two ways: it deepens our (A) ___ for others' feelings, and by making us happier it (B) ___ our will to carry out our duties.
choices: (A) empathy — (B) weakens
(A) contempt — (B) strengthens
(A) talent — (B) replaces
(A) empathy — (B) measures
(A) empathy — (B) strengthens
items.exp: 'through empathy'로 타인의 감정을 이해하고, 행복은 'a useful tool that strengthens the will to act'라고 했어요.

items.q: 밑줄 친 [less of a struggle]이 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은? (it widens our empathetic grasp of others, and it creates a state of mind in which living a good and ethical life becomes [less of a struggle].)
choices: It becomes easier to act morally.
Moral life loses all of its value.
People stop trying to be good.
Ethics becomes a matter of personal taste.
People argue less about music.

items.q: 다음 중 글의 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: lets a listener [glimpse] what other people are feeling
a cheerful person is more [inclined] to fulfill a duty
it is a useful tool that [weakens] the will to act
no one can become a better person without [growing] in this kind of emotional understanding
it [widens] our empathetic grasp of others

units.name: 171 Busy, Busy, Modern Life
units.passage: I draw inspiration from Bill Gates, who regularly steps away from his duties at Microsoft for seven days devoted solely to reading and thinking. Some years ago I took part in a question-and-answer event at the headquarters of his foundation, held just after he had returned from one of these so-called Think Weeks. I already knew the custom existed, but I was surprised to learn that it dated back to the very beginning of Microsoft and that he had never abandoned it, even while the company was growing at breakneck speed. Put differently, two times every year, in the most hectic and pressured period the firm had ever experienced, he still carved out a week to isolate himself and do nothing except read papers and books and investigate emerging technologies—an exercise that allowed him to see the larger picture. Because clearing an entire week from my own calendar feels daunting, if not impossible, I have instead built a miniature Think Week into every day, during mornings that are usually chaotic. For a short while, I protect a block of time for undisturbed reflection and serious study, and this habit lets me dive for pearls even in a rough sea.

items.q: 필자가 말하고자 하는 요지로 가장 알맞은 것은?
choices: 성공하려면 긴 휴가를 자주 떠나야 한다.
바쁜 일상 속에서도 짧게나마 깊이 생각하고 배우는 시간을 확보해야 한다.
기업이 성장하는 시기에는 업무에만 집중해야 한다.
새로운 기술은 책보다 현장에서 배우는 것이 낫다.
아침 시간은 운동에 쓰는 것이 가장 효과적이다.
items.exp: 필자는 Bill Gates의 Think Week에서 영감을 받아 바쁜 아침마다 방해받지 않는 성찰과 학습 시간을 만든다고 했어요.

items.q: Bill Gates의 Think Week에 관한 내용으로 일치하지 않는 것은?

마이크로소프트 초창기부터 시작되었다.
회사가 급성장하던 시기에도 계속되었다.
회사가 안정된 이후에야 처음 시작되었다.
그 기간 동안 글과 책을 읽고 신기술을 탐구했다.
items.exp: 'it dated back to the very beginning of Microsoft'라고 했으므로 초창기부터 시작되었어요. 안정된 이후에 시작되었다는 것은 틀려요.

바쁜 아침에 방해받지 않는 짧은 성찰과 학습 시간을 갖는다.
주말마다 기술 박람회에 간다.
Bill Gates의 강연 영상을 매일 시청한다.

completely necessary

Why Reading Is a Waste of a Busy Morning

Because mornings are the only time the writer is able to read.

Because a full week of reading seemed useless for the writer's work.

다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Inspired by Bill Gates, who kept taking a week for reading and thinking even during Microsoft's most (A) ___ years, the writer sets aside a short block of time each morning for (B) ___ reflection and study.

choices: earn money even when the company is struggling
escape from work by traveling to the ocean
take risks that most people would avoid

items.q: 다음 중 글의 문장을 옮긴 것으로 어법상 틀린 것은?
choices: Bill Gates, who regularly [steps] away from his duties

during mornings that [are] usually chaotic

units.name: 172 Digital Art
units.passage: Some forms of digital art, particularly works exhibited in galleries and museums through screens, computers, and interactive setups, are usually said to pose problems because they are immaterial: they depend on software and networks instead of canvas, stone, or other conventional media. Yet a large share of the actual trouble in showing and conserving such works stems from their physical side. Digital data, as strings of bits and bytes, are in the end easier to store and copy faithfully than paint or videotape. The difficulty lies elsewhere. Faster processors and sharper screens keep arriving on the market at an accelerating rate, and each new generation can drastically alter how a piece looks and behaves if it was originally designed for slower machines and coarser displays. Immateriality certainly lies at the heart of new media art, influencing both how artists create and how curators exhibit—but it can never be fully separated from the hardware through which the digital medium exists. Consequently, keeping digital artworks alive over the long term demands that museums continually update their equipment and technical systems so that they keep up with the speed of technological change.

items.q: 글의 제목으로 가장 알맞은 것은?
choices: Digital Art: A New Way to Express Oneself
Why Traditional Materials Still Dominate Art
The End of Museums in the Digital Age
Invisible Code, Physical Problems: Keeping Digital Art Alive
How Interactive Art Attracts More Visitors

네트워크 보안 문제

units.name: 173 Sports Themes
units.passage: Professional sports leagues used to reshape their games mainly to make them thrilling and hard to predict, hoping to draw the largest possible audience. American football, for instance, revised its rules to heighten suspense, producing high-scoring contests that suited the tastes of American fans, while dazzling halftime performances and odd promotional stunts were added so the sport could compete with other kinds of entertainment. Today, however, rule changes are shaped more and more by data analysis, new technology, and a more sophisticated knowledge of how fans actually behave. Major League Baseball, for example, adopted a pitch clock to make games move faster and keep spectators interested, a decision based on research indicating that people's attention spans are shrinking. Soccer, likewise, brought in VAR, the Video Assistant Referee system, to make officiating fairer and to cut down on disputes, answering calls from supporters as well as concerns about the integrity of competition. This change marks a deep transformation in the way professional sports are run: strategy, scientific evidence, and the game's health over the long run now occupy the central position, rather than spectacle alone.

units.name: 174 Environmental Strategies
units.passage: Wildfires are a tangled problem shaped by many environmental, social, and economic forces at once. A growing body of research points out that certain public policies have actually intensified the danger. A well-known case is the so-called set-aside paradox, which takes its name from a 1988 measure of the European Economic Community. The policy urged farmers to leave part of their fields uncultivated, both to cut Europe's overproduction of food and to ease the environmental harm caused by increasingly intensive farming. Despite these good intentions, the measure made vegetation more continuous across the countryside, because abandoned plots soon filled with grasses and weeds that burn readily, providing an unbroken path for flames. On top of this, many shrinking rural communities have turned to tourism in place of their traditional ways of using the land. In such places, practices meant to manage or reduce fuel, including controlled burning, may be opposed because they leave scars on scenery that visitors come to admire. At Arouca Geopark in Portugal, worries of this kind caused fuel reduction work to be halted in 2016, and the area later suffered the worst wildfire in its recorded history.

units.name: 175 Agent and Agency
units.passage: In animals and humans alike, the nervous system is a bodily organ like any other; it does not sit apart from the flesh the way a microprocessor runs on its own inside a robot. A robot's controlling chip draws only a tiny share of power when set beside the motors it directs. The human brain, by contrast, burns roughly 20 percent of all the energy the body uses, which suggests that it does far more than issue orders: it also responds. Once we recognize that the body's own shape and material makeup, along with its exchanges with the surroundings, handle part of the work of control, the line separating the controller from what it controls grows even fuzzier. Picture yourself jogging on a flat track that suddenly slopes gently downward. You speed up a little, yet not because your brain commands your legs to hurry. Gravity pulls your body forward, your limbs swing more quickly as a result, and this quicker motion in turn accelerates the rhythmic circuits inside your brain. Thus no one system is in charge. Brain and body steer each other's actions, exercising an agency that belongs to both of them together.

units.name: 176 Scientific Research
units.passage: Cosmologists run simulations everywhere these days: roughly a dozen independent codes exist, hundreds of new runs and research papers appear annually, and striking press releases come out by the score. Yet none of this activity means researchers are marching toward one ultimate model that reproduces the entire universe flawlessly. Reaching that degree of detail cannot be done, and it would hardly be worth doing anyway. What simulations really provide is a framework for organizing knowledge, insight, and joint research. No single scientist could build a simulation alone and then check it against the data gathered by a modern survey telescope, because the necessary expertise is enormous. It stretches across hydrodynamics, the birth of stars, the formation and growth of black holes, optics, quantum mechanics, and artificial intelligence, and each of these fields could absorb a whole career without ever being exhausted. This endlessness is precisely what makes simulation work so thrilling, but it also makes cooperation indispensable. The virtual universes that simulations produce are not their most rewarding outcome; such worlds remain pale copies of the real one, about as exciting as tomorrow's weather report. The true excitement belongs to people, for simulations allow scientists to express and test how separate ideas connect with one another.

units.name: 177 The Reach of Philosophy
units.passage: In his 1934 book Art as Experience, the philosopher John Dewey argued that genuine experiences unfold as unbroken episodes possessing their own pattern and structure. His examples ranged widely, from an argument with a close friend to a storm met in the middle of an Atlantic crossing. When such an episode draws to its end, Dewey claimed, it acquires an aesthetic quality that gathers it into an emotional whole, complete and unified. In this way he connected ordinary life with artistic experience, stressing the coherence and unity that we also admire in great paintings, plays, and films. Dewey further regarded doing and undergoing as two complementary ways in which we respond to circumstances. Sometimes we act deliberately (doing) in order to reach our goals and satisfy our wants. At other times we are swept up by intense situations (undergoing) that stir our feelings, tying basic physical reactions to vivid, specific memories of particular events. Extending this view, we can say that an artist or writer both produces an image or scene and feels its impact, and does so in a unified way. Such a lively exchange between the spontaneous inner role and the reflective outer role is what successful works of art depend on.

units.name: 178 Psychological Strategies
units.passage: Defensive pessimists always anticipate the worst outcome, worrying constantly and picturing every possible way things could go wrong. Suppose you belong to this group and must give an important speech in a week. You will probably persuade yourself that failure is inevitable. Rather than quitting, however, you transform that fear into a deliberate method known as defensive pessimism. When doubts about themselves begin to sneak in, these people refuse to let fear paralyze them. Instead, they purposely imagine a catastrophe in vivid detail, heightening their anxiety so that it can be turned into motivation. Having pictured the worst, they feel pushed to prevent it, so they examine every relevant detail to ensure they will not fail disastrously, and this careful checking gives them a feeling of control. Because their anxiety reaches its highest point well before the event, it pushes them to prepare thoroughly, and by the time the moment comes they are ready to do well. Their confidence, therefore, does not come from ignorance or from false beliefs about the challenges ahead, but from careful thought and serious preparation. Take away their anxiety and they lose interest; cheer them up and they stop planning. Oddly enough, the surest way to ruin the performance of a habitual defensive pessimist is to make that person happy.

units.name: 179 Evolution as a Puzzle
units.passage: Standard and extended evolutionary theory part ways most clearly over how adaptation works. The standard view treats adaptation as a reaction to pressures imposed from outside, whereas the extended view holds that organisms play an active part, reshaping their own selective environments through a process called niche construction so that conditions fit them better. Niche construction takes place whenever a creature changes its surroundings, either by altering the conditions around it or by relocating to a new habitat, and in doing so it places itself under a different set of selective pressures. Aquatic beetles that use plastron gills offer a remarkable illustration. These insects need air to breathe, yet they spend their lives under water without any body structure that works like a gill. Rather than relying on anatomy, they meet this challenge by constructing a niche: they take bubbles of air down with them, forming a kind of underwater aqualung. The air held between the beetle's body and the surrounding water serves as a private oxygen tank, letting the insect breathe while submerged. Over many generations, some species have even developed flattened legs close to the body that act as hydrofoils, helping water stream smoothly around the bubble and keeping it from shrinking.

units.name: 180 Ideologies in Everyday Life
units.passage: People tend to believe that a shared goal holds a group together, but common goals frequently split groups through what is called horizontal hostility: more radical members scorn moderate ones for being insufficiently pure. In one study, vegans displayed almost three times as much prejudice against less strict vegetarians as those vegetarians displayed against vegans. The vegans' reasoning was simple: if egg-eating vegetarians truly cared about animals, they would give up eggs. By contrast, researchers have found that strategic alignment can help create durable coalitions, at times mattering more than agreement on ideology. Although differences in belief like those between vegans and vegetarians can drive people apart, evidence suggests that engaging in the same methods can build unity. In one experiment, participants who sang their national anthem together at the same moment reported feeling more closely connected than participants who sang on their own or did not sing. Similarly, some sociologists observed that social movements using similar tactics were more inclined to form alliances, even when the causes at their core were different. If you have devoted years to joining protests, you may easily feel a shared identity with another group that works in the same manner.
